explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says, "Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah…" (Judges 11:29). After that, he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, then through Mizpah of Gilead. From there he advanced against the Ammonites.

I get why that one tempts you, friend. But this verse says the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah. No angel is mentioned here (Judges 11:29). The Spirit comes, and then Jephthah passes through Gilead and Manasseh on his way to the Ammonites.

explanations.answer: A deep sleep from the LORD
explanations.explanation: A deep sleep right before a battle? Jephthah would sleep through the whole thing, friend. The Bible does have a deep sleep from the LORD in another place, when He put Adam under (Genesis 2:21). Here it's different: the Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah, and then he advances against the Ammonites (Judges 11:29).

explanations.answer: Whatever comes out his door to greet him
explanations.explanation: You caught it, baker. Jephthah says, "…whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me on my triumphant return from the Ammonites will belong to the LORD…" (Judges 11:31). Notice how open that wording is. He doesn't name what it will be. I think it's worth slowing down on that line, because the story leans on it.

explanations.answer: The first lamb born in his flock
explanations.explanation: A lamb is a neat, specific promise, friend, and that's why it doesn't match. Jephthah never mentions a flock. He says "…whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me…" (Judges 11:31). A vow that open should make us lean in a little.

explanations.answer: A tenth of what he takes in battle
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like tidy accounting, baker. But the vow isn't about spoils at all. Jephthah says whatever comes out the door of his house to greet him will belong to the LORD (Judges 11:31). Nothing in the vow mentions a tenth.

True, baker. The text says, "So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD delivered them into his hand." (Judges 11:32). That's the very thing Jephthah's "If indeed" was asking for. The part of the vow that depended on the win has now happened.

The text actually says the opposite, friend. "…the LORD delivered them into his hand." (Judges 11:32). Jephthah's "If indeed" gets its answer, and the Ammonites are subdued before the Israelites (Judges 11:33). No close call, no hanging by a thread.

Yes, baker. The text says, "…there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing!" (Judges 11:34). She came out to meet him. I think this is where the story gets heavy, so let's take the next part gently.

I see why a servant sounds natural, friend, since a household has many people in it. But the text names his daughter as the one who comes out with tambourines and dancing (Judges 11:34). She's the one coming out to meet him.

The text never mentions a wife in this scene, baker. It says, "…there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing!" (Judges 11:34). Tambourines and dancing, and it's his daughter coming out to meet him. I think this is the moment the story turns.

The text says otherwise, friend. Right after she comes out, it adds, "She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her." (Judges 11:34). So there's no other child in the picture. She's the only one.

That's right, baker. "She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her." (Judges 11:34). The verse takes a moment to say so, and I think that tells us how much is on the line. This one is heavy.

explanations.answer: He gave his word to the LORD
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Jephthah says, "…for I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back." (Judges 11:35). His vow in verse 30 was made to the LORD. I think this one hurts, so let's go slowly.

explanations.answer: The elders of Gilead heard it
explanations.explanation: Jephthah doesn't point to the elders here, friend. He says, "…I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back." (Judges 11:35). His vow was made to the LORD (Judges 11:30), and in this verse he says nothing about who else heard it. I think this is a heavy moment for him.

explanations.answer: He swore it before his army
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention an army in connection with the vow, baker. Jephthah made his vow "…to the LORD…" (Judges 11:30). And when he sees his daughter, he says, "…I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back." (Judges 11:35). That's the reason he gives.

explanations.answer: The LORD avenged him of the Ammonites
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. She says, "you have given your word to the LORD. Do to me as you have said, for the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites." (Judges 11:36). She starts with the vow and then points to what the LORD just did. I think it's quite a moment, and what she says is remarkable.

explanations.answer: Israel needs a leader it can trust
explanations.explanation: That sounds sensible, friend, but she never says it. The text gives her reason: "…for the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites." (Judges 11:36). It's what the LORD has done that she points to.

explanations.answer: A vow made before battle is sacred
explanations.explanation: You're close to part of it, baker. She does say, "you have given your word to the LORD." But the reason she gives after "for" is, "…the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites." (Judges 11:36). She never says anything about when the vow was made.
Yes, baker. She asks to wander "…through the mountains with my friends…" (Judges 11:37). She doesn't ask to go alone. I think there's something tender in that.

I can see why you'd picture servants, friend, but the text doesn't mention any. She asks to wander for two months "…through the mountains with my friends…" (Judges 11:37). Those are the ones she wants beside her.
Sisters isn't the word in her request, baker. She asks to wander for two months "…through the mountains with my friends…" (Judges 11:37). Friends is the word the text gives.
The text says the opposite, friend. When she asks for two months, he answers, "Go," and he sent her away for two months (Judges 11:38). He grants her request.
That's right, baker. Jephthah answers her request with one word: "Go," and he sends her away for two months (Judges 11:38). She leaves with her friends. I think that one word carries a lot.
That's right, baker. The text says she "…mourned her virginity upon the mountains." (Judges 11:38). She left with her friends to do it. I think we should let that sit for a moment.

Celebrating isn't what this is, friend. Her own words are, "…mourn my virginity." (Judges 11:37). And the text says she "…mourned her virginity upon the mountains." (Judges 11:38). It's a time of sorrow.

Guarding isn't the word here, baker. She asks to "…mourn my virginity." (Judges 11:37), and the text says she "…mourned her virginity upon the mountains." (Judges 11:38). It's a time of mourning with her friends.

explanations.answer: Young women lament his daughter four days a year
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says it "has become a custom in Israel that each year the young women of Israel go out for four days to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite." (Judges 11:39-40). Her story wasn't forgotten. I think that's the heaviest line in the whole passage.

explanations.answer: Fathers stop making vows before a battle
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. The custom it names is that each year the young women of Israel "…go out for four days to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite." (Judges 11:40). It's about remembering her. Nothing is said about what fathers do.

explanations.answer: Families dance with tambourines every spring
explanations.explanation: The tambourines belong to her welcome in verse 34, baker, not to the custom. The custom is that each year the young women of Israel "…go out for four days to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite." (Judges 11:40). The text says four days each year and doesn't mention a season. It's a custom of lament.
